P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A cell, a bulb X, a bulb Y and two ammeters are joined in one loop: ammeter A1 between the cell and bulb X, ammeter A2 between bulb Y and the cell. Which is true when the bulbs glow?

a single loop has the same current everywhere (Topics 1 and 5).

Current is not used up; the bulbs take energy, not charge.
Nothing adds current between X and Y.
If A2 read zero, no current would flow anywhere in the loop and the bulbs would not glow.
One path → the same current through both ammeters.

Asked: how the current compares before and after the bulbs.

Concept used: a single loop has the same current everywhere (Topics 1 and 5).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Current is not used up; the bulbs take energy, not charge.
    • (b) ✘ Nothing adds current between X and Y.
    • (c) ✘ If A2 read zero, no current would flow anywhere in the loop and the bulbs would not glow.
    • (d) ✔ One path → the same current through both ammeters.

  2. Answer (d)

P2● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A cell is connected to a resistor. Which statement is correct?

conventional current and electron flow (Topic 1).

Electrons are negative; they leave from the − terminal.
That is the direction of the electrons.
They move in opposite directions.
Conventional current: from + round the outside circuit to −.

Asked: the correct statement about directions.

Concept used: conventional current and electron flow (Topic 1).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Electrons are negative; they leave from the − terminal.
    • (b) ✘ That is the direction of the electrons.
    • (c) ✘ They move in opposite directions.
    • (d) ✔ Conventional current: from + round the outside circuit to −.

  2. Answer (d)

ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel (Topics 1 and 2).

A voltmeter in series does not measure the p.d. across the lamp.
An ammeter in parallel does not carry the lamp's current.

Asked: how to connect the two meters.

Concept used: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel (Topics 1 and 2).

    • (b) ✘ The two connections are swapped.
    • (c) ✘ A voltmeter in series does not measure the p.d. across the lamp.
    • (d) ✘ An ammeter in parallel does not carry the lamp's current.

  2. Answer (a)

P6● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

For resistors connected in parallel, which quantity is the same for every resistor?

parallel rules (Topic 5).

The current divides: more through the smaller resistor.
All are joined between the same two points, so the p.d. is the same.
Heat per second =V2R= \dfrac{V^2}{R}=RV2​ differs when RRR differs.
Power =V2R= \dfrac{V^2}{R}=RV2​ differs too.

Asked: what is common in parallel.

Concept used: parallel rules (Topic 5).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ The current divides: more through the smaller resistor.
    • (b) ✔ All are joined between the same two points, so the p.d. is the same.
    • (c) ✘ Heat per second =V2R= \dfrac{V^2}{R}=RV2​ differs when RRR differs.
    • (d) ✘ Power =V2R= \dfrac{V^2}{R}=RV2​ differs too.

  2. Answer (b)

P10●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Meera says: "In a torch, the current gets smaller after it passes through the bulb, because the bulb uses some of it up." (a) Is she right? (b) What does the bulb actually take from the moving charges?

Full solution

Given: a single loop: cells, bulb, switch. Asked: whether current is used up; what the bulb takes.

Concept used: current in a single loop; the cell supplies energy to the charges (Topics 1 and 2). Why it applies: the torch is one closed path.

  1. 1

    (a) Same current everywhere → in one loop, every coulomb that leaves the cell comes back to it; an ammeter placed before or after the bulb gives the same reading. So she is wrong.

  2. 2

    (b) Energy → the cell gives each coulomb energy (VVV joules per coulomb); in the bulb this energy becomes heat and light. The charges are not used up.

  3. Check: your textbook adds that we pay the electricity company for energy, not for electrons ✔.

  4. Answer (a) No — the current is the same in every part of the loop. (b) Energy: the bulb changes the electrical energy carried by the charges into heat and light.

    Write it in the exam (2 marks):

    (a) No; in a single (series) loop the current is the same everywhere. (1) (b) The bulb takes electrical energy from the charges (changing it to heat and light), not the charges themselves. (1)

    Common trap: "the bulb uses up electrons". Electrons are not consumed.

You got 0 of 2 parts.

P11●● StandardDiagram-based · 2 marksOriginal

Draw a circuit diagram of a cell, a closed plug key and a resistor in one loop. On it, mark (a) the direction of the conventional current with an arrow labelled I, and (b) the direction of electron flow with an arrow labelled "electrons".

Full solution

Given: cell, key, resistor in series. Asked: the diagram with both directions.

Concept used: symbols; conventional current vs electron flow (Topics 1 and 2). Why it applies: the two arrows must point opposite ways.

  1. 1

    Draw a ruled rectangle with the cell (long line +, short thick line −), the closed key (•) and the resistor (zig-zag).

  2. 2

    (a) Arrow I → leaving the cell's + terminal, through the resistor, back to the − terminal.

  3. 3

    (b) Electron arrow → the opposite way: from the − terminal, through the resistor, to the + terminal.

  4. Check: the two arrows point in opposite directions on every wire ✔.

  5. Answer Diagram as described: I from + round to −; electrons from − round to +.

    Write it in the exam (2 marks):

    Correct symbols in one loop (1); I from + to − outside the cell and electrons in the opposite direction (1)

    Common trap: drawing the long line of the cell as −. The long line is +.

P12●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AAn ammeter is always connected in series in the circuit through which the current is to be measured.
RAn ammeter must have the whole current that is to be measured passing through it.
ammeter connection (Topic 1).

Asked: the truth of A and R, and whether R explains A.

Concept used: ammeter connection (Topic 1).

  1. Reasoning: A is true — your textbook says the ammeter is always connected in series in the circuit through which the current is to be measured. R is true — an ammeter measures the current that passes through it. R explains A: only a meter placed in series, in the path of the current, has that whole current passing through it.

  2. Answer (A)

    (c) Energy.

P14●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AA long, thin copper wire and a short, thick copper wire have different resistances but the same resistivity.
RResistivity is a characteristic property of the material of the conductor.
resistance vs resistivity (Topic 4).

Asked: the truth of A and R, and whether R explains A.

Concept used: resistance vs resistivity (Topic 4).

  1. Reasoning: A is true: R=ρlAR = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}R=ρAl​ — different lll and AAA give different RRR, but both are copper. R is true (your textbook's own words) and it explains why the resistivity is the same: it depends only on the material (at a given temperature), not on the shape.

  2. Answer (A)

P15●● StandardNumerical · 2 marksOriginal

A wire has a resistance of 32 Ω. Find the resistance of a wire of the same material that (a) has the same length but half the diameter, (b) is twice as long and has twice the diameter.

Full solution

Given: R=32 ΩR = 32\ \OmegaR=32 Ω. Asked: RRR for two new wires.

Concept used: R∝lAR \propto \dfrac{l}{A}R∝Al​ and A∝d2A \propto d^2A∝d2 (Topic 4). Why it applies: same material, so only lll and ddd matter.

  1. 1

    (a) Half the diameter → area (12)2=14\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}(21​)2=41​ → resistance ×4.

    R=4×32 Ω=128 ΩR = 4 \times 32\ \Omega = 128\ \OmegaR=4×32 Ω=128 ΩSwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    (b) Length ×2 → resistance ×2; diameter ×2 → area ×4 → resistance ÷4.

    R=32×24 Ω=16 ΩR = 32 \times \dfrac{2}{4}\ \Omega = 16\ \OmegaR=32×42​ Ω=16 ΩSwipe to see the whole equation →

  3. Check: (b) lA\dfrac{l}{A}Al​ changes by 24=12\dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}42​=21​, so RRR halves ✔.

  4. Answer (a) 128 Ω128\ \Omega128 Ω (b) 16 Ω16\ \Omega16 Ω

    Write it in the exam (2 marks):

    (a) AAA becomes 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ → R=4×32=128 ΩR = 4 \times 32 = 128\ \OmegaR=4×32=128 Ω (1) (b) R=32×24=16 ΩR = 32 \times \dfrac{2}{4} = 16\ \OmegaR=32×42​=16 Ω (1)

    Common trap: (a) "half the diameter → double the resistance" (64 Ω). Area depends on the square of the diameter.

    (a) Same p.d. across each.

    I1=7 V14 Ω=0.5 A,I2=7 V35 Ω=0.2 AI_1 = \dfrac{7\ \text{V}}{14\ \Omega} = 0.5\ \text{A}, \qquad I_2 = \dfrac{7\ \text{V}}{35\ \Omega} = 0.2\ \text{A}I1​=14 Ω7 V​=0.5 A,I2​=35 Ω7 V​=0.2 ASwipe to see the whole equation →

    (b) Currents add.

    I=0.5 A+0.2 A=0.7 AI = 0.5\ \text{A} + 0.2\ \text{A} = 0.7\ \text{A}I=0.5 A+0.2 A=0.7 ASwipe to see the whole equation →

    (c) Product over sum (two resistors).

    Rp=14×3514+35 Ω=49049 Ω=10 ΩR_p = \dfrac{14 \times 35}{14 + 35}\ \Omega = \dfrac{490}{49}\ \Omega = 10\ \OmegaRp​=14+3514×35​ Ω=49490​ Ω=10 ΩSwipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: VRp=710=0.7\dfrac{V}{R_p} = \dfrac{7}{10} = 0.7Rp​V​=107​=0.7 A ✔; 10 Ω < 14 Ω ✔.

P19●● StandardNumerical · 3 marksOriginal

An electric iron of resistance 55 Ω is connected to the 220 V mains for 10 minutes. Find (a) the current, (b) the heat produced.

Full solution

Given: R=55 ΩR = 55\ \OmegaR=55 Ω; V=220 VV = 220\ \text{V}V=220 V; t=10 mint = 10\ \text{min}t=10 min. Asked: III; HHH.

Concept used: I=VRI = \dfrac{V}{R}I=RV​, then H=I2RtH = I^2RtH=I2Rt (Topics 3 and 6). Why it applies: your textbook's advice — find the current first, then use Joule's law.

  1. 1

    (a) Current.

    I=220 V55 Ω=4 AI = \dfrac{220\ \text{V}}{55\ \Omega} = 4\ \text{A}I=55 Ω220 V​=4 ASwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Time in seconds.

    t=10×60 s=600 st = 10 \times 60\ \text{s} = 600\ \text{s}t=10×60 s=600 sSwipe to see the whole equation →

    (b) Heat.

the electric fuse (Topic 6).

P25●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: The kitchen circuit

A kitchen circuit works at 220 V and is protected by a 10 A fuse. On it are a mixer of 660 W, an electric kettle of 1540 W and a toaster of 880 W, all connected in parallel. The kettle is used for 15 minutes every day.

(a) Find the normal current of each appliance. (1)
(b) Can the mixer and the kettle be used together? What happens if the toaster is also switched on? (1)
(c) Find the cost of using the kettle for 30 days at Rs 7 per unit. (1)
(d) Give two reasons why the appliances are connected in parallel. (1)

Full solution

Given: 220 V; fuse 10 A; 660 W, 1540 W, 880 W in parallel; kettle 15 min/day. Asked: currents; fuse behaviour; cost; reasons for parallel.

Concept used: I=PVI = \dfrac{P}{V}I=VP​; currents add in parallel; units and cost; advantages of parallel (Topics 5–7). Why it applies: everything is on one parallel circuit behind one fuse.

  1. 1

    (a) Currents. Mixer 660220=3\dfrac{660}{220} = 3220660​=3 A; kettle 1540220=7\dfrac{1540}{220} = 72201540​=7 A; toaster 880220=4\dfrac{880}{220} = 4220880​=4 A.

  2. 2

    (b) Mixer + kettle → 3+7=103 + 7 = 103+7=10 A. This does not exceed the 10 A rating, so yes — the fuse does not melt, but there is no safety margin.

  3. 3

    All three → 3+7+4=143 + 7 + 4 = 143+7+4=14 A, more than 10 A → the fuse wire melts and the circuit breaks.

  4. 4

    (c) Kettle energy in 30 days: 1.54 kW×0.25 h×30=11.551.54\ \text{kW} \times 0.25\ \text{h} \times 30 = 11.551.54 kW×0.25 h×30=11.55 kW h.

  5. 5

    Cost: 11.55×Rs 7=Rs 80.8511.55 \times \text{Rs }7 = \text{Rs }80.8511.55×Rs 7=Rs 80.85.

  6. 6

    (d) In parallel each appliance gets the full 220 V, and each can be switched on or off independently (one failing does not stop the others).

  7. Check: total power for all three = 660+1540+880=3080660 + 1540 + 880 = 3080660+1540+880=3080 W, and 3080220=14\dfrac{3080}{220} = 142203080​=14 A ✔.

  8. Answer (a) 3 A, 7 A, 4 A (b) yes — 10 A does not exceed the 10 A rating (no margin); with the toaster as well, 14 A — the fuse melts (c) 11.55 units, Rs 80.85 (d) full p.d. to each; independent working

    Write it in the exam (4 marks):

    1 mark for each of (a)–(d).

    Common trap: (c) using 15 (minutes) as hours. 15 min = 0.25 h.

P26●●● AdvancedNumerical · 3 marksOriginal

A wire of resistance 9 Ω is stretched uniformly until its length is doubled. Assume that its volume (and its material) stays the same. Find (a) its new resistance, (b) its new resistivity compared with the old.

Full solution

Given: R1=9 ΩR_1 = 9\ \OmegaR1​=9 Ω; l2=2l1l_2 = 2l_1l2​=2l1​; volume unchanged. Asked: R2R_2R2​; resistivity.

Concept used: R=ρlAR = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}R=ρAl​; volume =A×l= A \times l=A×l (Topic 4). Why it applies: stretching changes both the length and the area. (The "same volume" step is an extra assumption the question gives you; your textbook's formula then does the rest.)

  1. 1

    Volume the same → A1l1=A2l2=A2(2l1)A_1 l_1 = A_2 l_2 = A_2 (2l_1)A1​l1​=A2​l2​=A2​(2l1​), so A2=A12A_2 = \dfrac{A_1}{2}A2​=2A1​​.

  2. 2

    New resistance.

    R2=ρ2l1A1/2=4×ρl1A1=4R1R_2 = \rho \dfrac{2l_1}{A_1/2} = 4 \times \rho\dfrac{l_1}{A_1} = 4R_1R2​=ρA1​/22l1​​=4×ρA1​l1​​=4R1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Substitute.

    R2=4×9 Ω=36 ΩR_2 = 4 \times 9\ \Omega = 36\ \OmegaR2​=4×9 Ω=36 ΩSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    (b) Resistivity → same material (and temperature) → unchanged.

  5. Check: length ×2 alone would double RRR; the area halving doubles it again: ×4 ✔.

  6. Answer (a) 36 Ω36\ \Omega36 Ω (b) the resistivity is unchanged.

    Write it in the exam (3 marks):

    A2=A12A_2 = \dfrac{A_1}{2}A2​=2A1​​ (volume constant) (1); R2=ρ2lA/2=4R=36 ΩR_2 = \rho\dfrac{2l}{A/2} = 4R = 36\ \OmegaR2​=ρA/22l​=4R=36 Ω (1); resistivity unchanged (same material) (1)

    Common trap: answering 18 Ω — doubling the length but forgetting that the wire also gets thinner.

P28●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: A suspicious reading

In Practical 4, Kabir records these readings for a resistance wire:

III (A) 0.1 0.2 0.3 0.4
VVV (V) 1.4 2.8 4.9 5.6

His teacher says one reading is probably wrong.

(a) Work out VI\dfrac{V}{I}IV​ for each reading. Which reading is likely to be wrong? (1)
(b) What is the resistance of the wire? (1)
(c) What should the wrong voltmeter reading have been? (1)
(d) Why should the key be taken out between readings? (1)

Full solution

Given: four pairs of readings. Asked: the odd reading; RRR; the corrected reading; why remove the key.

Concept used: Ohm's law — constant VI\dfrac{V}{I}IV​ at constant temperature (Topic 3). Why it applies: this is the Practical 4 analysis.

  1. 1

    (a) Ratios: 1.40.1=14\dfrac{1.4}{0.1} = 140.11.4​=14, 2.80.2=14\dfrac{2.8}{0.2} = 140.22.8​=14, 4.90.3≈16.3\dfrac{4.9}{0.3} \approx 16.30.34.9​≈16.3, 5.60.4=14\dfrac{5.6}{0.4} = 140.45.6​=14 (Ω). The third reading does not fit.

  2. 2

    (b) Resistance from the three that agree → 14 Ω.

  3. 3

    (c) Corrected reading → V=IR=0.3×14=4.2V = IR = 0.3 \times 14 = 4.2V=IR=0.3×14=4.2 V.

  4. 4

    (d) A current heats the wire; Ohm's law holds only if the temperature stays the same, so the key is taken out between readings to let the wire cool.

  5. Check: on a graph, the third point would sit clearly above the straight line through the other three ✔.

  6. Answer (a) 14, 14, about 16.3, 14 Ω — the third reading (b) 14 Ω14\ \Omega14 Ω (c) 4.2 V4.2\ \text{V}4.2 V (d) to stop the wire heating up, so that its temperature (and resistance) stays the same

    Write it in the exam (4 marks):

    1 mark for each of (a)–(d).

    Common trap: (b) averaging all four ratios (14.6 Ω), including the wrong one.

A room heater has two identical coils, each of resistance 55 Ω. A switch lets you use one coil alone, both in series, or both in parallel, always on 220 V. Find the power in each setting and say which setting gives the most heat.

Given: two coils of 55 Ω; V=220 VV = 220\ \text{V}V=220 V. Asked: power for one coil, series, parallel.

Concept used: series and parallel; P=V2RP = \dfrac{V^2}{R}P=RV2​ (Topics 5 and 7). Why it applies: the p.d. is fixed, so less resistance means more power.

  1. 1

    One coil.

    P=220255 W=4840055 W=880 WP = \dfrac{220^2}{55}\ \text{W} = \dfrac{48400}{55}\ \text{W} = 880\ \text{W}P=552202​ W=5548400​ W=880 WSwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Series: R=110 ΩR = 110\ \OmegaR=110 Ω.

    P=48400110 W=440 WP = \dfrac{48400}{110}\ \text{W} = 440\ \text{W}P=11048400​ W=440 WSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Parallel: R=27.5 ΩR = 27.5\ \OmegaR=27.5 Ω.

    P=4840027.5 W=1760 WP = \dfrac{48400}{27.5}\ \text{W} = 1760\ \text{W}P=27.548400​ W=1760 WSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Most heat → the parallel setting.

  5. Check: series doubles RRR → half the power; parallel halves RRR → double the power (440=880÷2440 = 880 \div 2440=880÷2; 1760=880×21760 = 880 \times 21760=880×2) ✔.

  6. Answer One coil 880 W; series 440 W; parallel 1760 W — the parallel setting gives the most heat.

    Write it in the exam (3 marks):

    One coil 880 W (1); series 440 W (1); parallel 1760 W — most heat (1)

    A carries the full current III; its limit: I2×2=18I^2 \times 2 = 18I2×2=18.

    B and C each carry half: 1.5 A, giving 1.52×2=4.51.5^2 \times 2 = 4.51.52×2=4.5 W each — well within 18 W.

Given: an ammeter, connected in series. Asked: low or high resistance, with a reason.

Concept used: series resistances add; I=VRI = \dfrac{V}{R}I=RV​ (Topics 3 and 5). Why it applies: the ammeter becomes part of the series chain.

  1. 1

    The ammeter is in series, so its resistance adds to the circuit's resistance.

  2. 2

    A large added resistance would reduce the very current it is trying to measure.

  3. 3

    So it should be very low — ideally zero.

  4. Check: a near-zero resistance leaves the current unchanged ✔.

  5. Answer Low (ideally zero) — being in series, any resistance it has would reduce the current it measures.

    Write it in the exam (2 marks):

    Low (1); it is in series, so a high resistance would change (reduce) the current being measured (1)

Draw a circuit diagram of an electric circuit containing a cell, a key, an ammeter, a resistor of 2 Ω in series with a combination of two resistors (4 Ω each) in parallel and a voltmeter across the parallel combination. Will the potential difference across the 2 Ω resistor be the same as that across the parallel combination of 4Ω resistors? Give reason.

Full solution

Given: cell, key, ammeter, 2 Ω in series with (4 Ω ∥ 4 Ω), voltmeter across the pair. Asked: the diagram; whether the two p.d.s are equal.

Concept used: parallel combination; series → same current (Topic 5). Why it applies: compare the 2 Ω resistor with the pair's equivalent.

  1. 1

    Diagram → one loop: cell, key, ammeter (series), the 2 Ω resistor, then the two 4 Ω resistors side by side between two junctions; the voltmeter joined across the two junctions.

  2. 2

    Pair: 4×44+4=2 Ω\dfrac{4 \times 4}{4 + 4} = 2\ \Omega4+44×4​=2 Ω.

  3. 3

    Same current through the 2 Ω resistor and the pair (series), and same resistance (2 Ω each) → V=IRV = IRV=IR is the same for both.

  4. Check: each takes half of the cell's p.d. ✔.

  5. Answer Yes — the parallel pair is equivalent to 2 Ω, and it carries the same current as the 2 Ω resistor, so V=IRV = IRV=IR gives the same p.d. across both.

E23● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Electricity, SA 23

How does use of a fuse wire protect electrical appliances?

Full solution

Given: a fuse in series with an appliance. Asked: how it protects.

Concept used: the electric fuse (Topic 6). Why it applies: the fuse uses the heating effect.

  1. 1

    The fuse wire is in series with the appliance, so it carries the same current.

  2. 2

    If the current becomes larger than the rated value, the wire heats up (H=I2RtH = I^2RtH=I2Rt) and melts.

  3. 3

    The circuit breaks, the current stops, and the appliance is protected.

  4. Check: this is why the fuse's melting point must be suitable — not too high ✔.

  5. Answer The fuse wire is in series with the appliance; an unduly high current heats it to its melting point, it melts and breaks the circuit, so the high current cannot damage the appliance.

    Write it in the exam (2 marks):

    Fuse in series; a current above its rating heats the wire to its melting point (1); it melts and breaks the circuit, stopping the current (1)

E24●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Electricity, SA 24

What is electrical resistivity? In a series electrical circuit comprising a resistor made up of a metallic wire, the ammeter reads 5 A. The reading of the ammeter decreases to half when the length of the wire is doubled. Why?

Full solution

Given: ammeter 5 A; length doubled → 2.5 A. Asked: resistivity; the reason for halving.

Concept used: R=ρlAR = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}R=ρAl​; I=VRI = \dfrac{V}{R}I=RV​ (Topics 3 and 4). Why it applies: the same source, a longer wire.

  1. 1

    Resistivity → the constant ρ\rhoρ in R=ρlAR = \rho\dfrac{l}{A}R=ρAl​; it is the resistance of a wire of the material of unit length and unit area of cross-section (unit Ω m), and depends only on the material (and temperature).

  2. 2

    Length doubled → R∝lR \propto lR∝l, so the resistance doubles.

  3. 3

    Same p.d. → I=VRI = \dfrac{V}{R}I=RV​, so the current halves (5 A → 2.5 A).

  4. Check: this is exactly the observation in Activity 11.3 ✔.

  5. Answer Resistivity is the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit area of cross-section of a material (unit Ω m). Doubling the length doubles the resistance (R∝lR \propto lR∝l), so with the same p.d. the current falls to half (I=VRI = \dfrac{V}{R}I=RV​).

    Write it in the exam (3 marks):

    Definition of resistivity (1); R∝lR \propto lR∝l, so R doubles (1); I=VRI = \dfrac{V}{R}I=RV​ halves (1)

E26●● StandardNumerical · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Electricity, SA 26

A current of 1 ampere flows in a series circuit containing an electric lamp and a conductor of 5 Ω when connected to a 10 V battery. Calculate the resistance of the electric lamp.
Now if a resistance of 10 Ω is connected in parallel with this series combination, what change (if any) in current flowing through 5 Ω conductor and potential difference across the lamp will take place? Give reason.

Full solution

Given: I=1 AI = 1\ \text{A}I=1 A; lamp + 5 Ω in series; V=10 VV = 10\ \text{V}V=10 V; then 10 Ω across the series combination. Asked: lamp resistance; changes.

Concept used: series total; parallel branches each get the full p.d. (Topic 5). Why it applies: the 10 Ω is a new branch across the same battery.

  1. 1

    Total resistance. R=VI=101=10 ΩR = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{10}{1} = 10\ \OmegaR=IV​=110​=10 Ω.

  2. 2

    Lamp. Rlamp=10−5=5 ΩR_{\text{lamp}} = 10 - 5 = 5\ \OmegaRlamp​=10−5=5 Ω.

  3. 3

    Adding 10 Ω in parallel → the lamp-and-conductor branch still has the same 10 V across it and the same 10 Ω, so its current stays 1 A.

  4. 4

    So the current through the 5 Ω conductor is unchanged (1 A), and the p.d. across the lamp is unchanged (1×5=51 \times 5 = 51×5=5 V). (The battery now supplies an extra 1 A through the new 10 Ω branch.)

  5. Check: this assumes the battery keeps its 10 V, as in all your textbook's problems ✔.

  6. Answer Lamp resistance 5 Ω5\ \Omega5 Ω. No change: the current through the 5 Ω conductor stays 1 A and the p.d. across the lamp stays 5 V, because a parallel branch does not change the p.d. across the original branch.

    Write it in the exam (3 marks):

    R=101=10 ΩR = \dfrac{10}{1} = 10\ \OmegaR=110​=10 Ω, lamp =5 Ω= 5\ \Omega=5 Ω (1); no change in current through 5 Ω (1); no change in p.d. across the lamp — same 10 V across the branch (1)

E29●● StandardLong answer · 5 marksNCERT Exemplar Electricity, LA 29

Three incandescent bulbs of 100 W each are connected in series in an electric circuit. In another circuit another set of three bulbs of the same wattage are connected in parallel to the same source.
(a) Will the bulb in the two circuits glow with the same brightness? Justify your answer.
(b) Now let one bulb in both the circuits get fused. Will the rest of the bulbs continue to glow in each circuit? Give reason.

Full solution

Given: three identical 100 W bulbs in series; three in parallel; same source. Asked: brightness compared; effect of one fused bulb.

Concept used: series vs parallel; P=V2RP = \dfrac{V^2}{R}P=RV2​ (Topics 5 and 7). Why it applies: identical bulbs, different arrangements.

  1. 1

    (a) Series: total resistance 3R3R3R; current one-third of a single bulb's; each bulb gets one-third of the p.d., so its power is (13)2=19\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{9}(31​)2=91​ of the rated power.

  2. 2

    Parallel: each bulb gets the full p.d. and uses its rated power.

  3. 3

    So No — the bulbs in parallel glow much more brightly.

  4. 4

    (b) Series: one fused bulb breaks the only path → current zero → all go out.

  5. 5

    Parallel: the other branches still have the full p.d. → they keep glowing with the same brightness.

  6. Check: the Exemplar key: series current is one-third, parallel bulbs glow more brightly; series bulbs stop, parallel bulbs continue ✔.

  7. Answer (a) No — in series each bulb has only one-third of the p.d. (and one-third of the current), so it glows far less brightly than a bulb in parallel, which has the full p.d. (b) In series the others go out (circuit broken); in parallel the others continue to glow normally (each has its own path and the full p.d.).

    Write it in the exam (5 marks):

    (a) No (1); series: R becomes 3R, current one-third, each bulb dim (1); parallel: each bulb at full p.d., normal brightness (1) (b) series: circuit broken, all stop (1); parallel: others glow as before (1)

E30●● StandardLong answer · 5 marksNCERT Exemplar Electricity, LA 30

State Ohm's law? How can it be verified experimentally? Does it hold good under all conditions? Comment.

Full solution

Given: —. Asked: the law; an experiment; its limits.

Concept used: Ohm's law and Activity 11.1 (Topic 3). Why it applies: this is Practical 4.

  1. 1

    Law → the p.d. across the ends of a metallic wire is directly proportional to the current through it, provided its temperature remains the same: V=IRV = IRV=IR.

  2. 2

    Experiment → circuit of Fig 11.2: nichrome wire XY, ammeter in series, voltmeter across XY, key, battery. Use 1, 2, 3 and 4 cells; record III and VVV each time (take the key out between readings); find VI\dfrac{V}{I}IV​ — it stays nearly constant; the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin.

  3. 3

    Not under all conditions → it holds only while the temperature stays the same; if the wire heats up, its resistance changes and VI\dfrac{V}{I}IV​ is no longer constant. (Your textbook states the law for a metallic wire at constant temperature; it does not claim more.)

  4. Check: the Exemplar key: "Ohm's law does not hold under all conditions. Mention the conditions." ✔.

  5. Answer Ohm's law: V∝IV \propto IV∝I (V = IR) for a metallic conductor at constant temperature. Verified with the Fig 11.2 circuit by taking several readings and showing that VI\dfrac{V}{I}IV​ is constant and the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin. It holds only if the temperature (and other physical conditions) of the conductor stay the same.

    Write it in the exam (5 marks):

    Statement with condition (1); labelled circuit diagram (1); method — several readings with 1–4 cells, VI\dfrac{V}{I}IV​ constant (1); straight-line V–I graph through the origin (1); not valid if the temperature changes (1)

How will you infer with the help of an experiment that the same current flows through every part of the circuit containing three resistances in series connected to a battery?

    Observation → the reading is the same in every position.

  4. 4

    Inference → the same current flows through every part of a series circuit.

  5. Check: this is your textbook's Activity 11.4 ✔.

What is Joule's heating effect? How can it be demonstrated experimentally? List its four applications in daily life.

  1. 1

    Joule's heating effect → when a current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is changed into heat; H=I2RtH = I^2RtH=I2Rt.

    Demonstration (a simple one; your textbook gives no activity for it) → connect a short piece of nichrome wire to a battery through a key and an ammeter; after a short time the wire becomes hot (or a little wax on it melts); with more cells (more current) it heats faster.
